root_cause: Cycle 12 MemoryStore used a plain sqlite3 database plus an AES-256-GCM encrypted snapshot. The snapshot pattern added migration complexity and did not provide native page-level encryption. During Cycle 15 migration to SQLCipher, the durable-memory e2e test failed because TriOSEncryption generated a fresh key on each Keychain access when Keychain reads returned errSecNotAvailable (-25320) in the non-UI test context, so the reloaded store keyed the same file with a different key and SQLite reported 'file is not a database'.
fix_pattern: Replace the encrypted snapshot with native SQLCipher page-level encryption via a new SQLCipherMemoryStore helper. Open databases with PRAGMA key using the Keychain-backed raw key, validate with PRAGMA cipher_version, migrate existing plaintext DBs and legacy .enc snapshots in place, switch journal mode to WAL with stale -wal/-shm cleanup, and checkpoint WAL before close. Cache the symmetric key inside TriOSEncryption so every caller in the same process uses the identical key, eliminating per-call Keychain drift in CLI tests and improving app runtime efficiency.
lessons: Keychain-backed keys can return errSecNotAvailable in non-UI contexts; in-process caching is required for deterministic SQLCipher keying in tests.
SQLCipher WAL mode is safe because WAL pages are encrypted, but stale plaintext -wal/-shm siblings must be removed before opening an encrypted database.
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) before sqlite3_close_v2 is necessary for a subsequent process (or reloaded instance) to see a consistent encrypted file.
Native SQLCipher page-level encryption is simpler and more robust than application-layer encrypted snapshots.
All Trinity gates must be re-run after key-management changes because key drift surfaces only on reopen, not on first write.
